title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 290
paragraphs: There is, moreover, a region in Arabia situated nearly opposite the city of Buto, to which place I came to inquire about the winged serpents. When I arrived I saw bones of serpents and spines in such great quantity that it is impossible to report the number; there were heaps of spines, some large, others less large, others smaller still, and these heaps were many. This region, where the spines are scattered upon the ground, is of the nature of an entrance from a narrow mountain pass into a great plain, which plain adjoins the plain of Egypt. The story goes that at the beginning of spring winged serpents fly from Arabia towards Egypt, and the birds called ibises meet them at the entrance to this country and do not suffer the serpents to pass by, but kill them. On account of this deed, the Arabians say, the ibis has come to be greatly honoured by the Egyptians; and the Egyptians also agree that it is for this reason that they honour these birds.
